title: Giant clams survive, thrive in Batangas marine sanctuaries
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY -- Giant clams (Tridacna gigas) seeded in the municipal waters off Lian and Nasugbu in Batangas province more than a decade ago continue to survive and thrive in protected marine areas.

In a report on Friday, Aug. 7, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR)-Calabarzon said giant clams planted in 2015 and 2016 in locally managed marine sanctuaries and protected areas in the two municipalities remain healthy.

The giant clams were seeded through the efforts of the DENR's Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) in Calaca in partnership with local communities and other stakeholders.

READ: Cadiz City goes after giant clams' killers

"Based on the latest monitoring, the giant clams have reached an average length of 2.25 feet," the DENR said.

The agency said the giant clams remain safe within the marine sanctuaries through the continuing protection and monitoring efforts of CENRO-Calaca and its local partners.

Locally known as "taklobo," the giant clam is the world's largest bivalve mollusk. It is classified as critically endangered on the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

Giant clams are also protected under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), an international agreement among governments designed to ensure that trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival.

The harvesting, selling, purchasing, and transporting of giant clams is prohibited under Republic Act No. 10654, or the Philippine Fisheries Code.

Beyond their value as food, giant clams are also targeted for their massive shells, which have been used as materials for jewelry, chandeliers, religious icons and other products.

Their valuable shells have made the endangered species a target of illegal trade, with some smugglers reportedly turning to giant clams as substitutes for ivory.

title: Need for emergency feeding of children, part 2
content_lead:
The Philippine government has several programs to combat child undernutrition. The two largest are the Supplementary Feeding Program (SFP) of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and the School-Based Feeding Program (SBFP) of the Department of Education (DepEd). The SFP targets children three to five years old enrolled in Child Development Centers (daycare centers) and Supervised Neighborhood Play groups.

The program provides daily nutritious hot meals (and, in some areas, milk) for 180 feeding days in 2026. It includes nutrition education for parents and caregivers, along with regular monitoring of the children’s weight and nutritional status. Local government units (LGUs) get involved under the Masustansyang Pagkain para sa Batang Pilipino Act. This year, the DSWD expanded the program to serve more than 1.8 million children nationwide, backed by a larger budget and a longer feeding period.

DepEd’s School-Based Feeding Program focuses on public school learners, especially those identified as wasted, severely wasted, or otherwise nutritionally at-risk. The program provides daily nutritious meals during the school year, milk feeding in many schools, and regular health and nutrition assessments. On July 8, 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced the nationwide expansion of the school feeding program, stating that the government intends to broaden coverage so that more learners receive nutritious meals while also supporting the Filipino farmers who supply the food. True enough, this program was given prominence in his State of the Nation Address (SONA) yesterday.

The government also supports child nutrition through the National Nutrition Council and the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition. Maternal and child nutrition services of the Department of Health include breastfeeding promotion, micronutrient supplementation, growth monitoring, deworming, and nutrition counseling. Additionally, local government units have their own community nutrition and food security initiatives. One of the most successful was implemented in Quezon Province when now-Congressman Jay Suarez was governor. Quezon Province was one of the pioneers in implementing the First 1,000 Days program, feeding the baby even while still in the womb of the mother.

Because of the magnitude of this problem of child stunting due to undernutrition, the private sector must do its share in ensuring that vulnerable children receive adequate nourishment during their critical years of growth and learning. That is why the Philippine Food Bank Foundation decided to partner with a public school in Muntinlupa in a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) program called “Balik Lusog.”

It was launched at Poblacion Elementary School in Muntinlupa in partnership with the Loaves and Fish Foundation, made possible by a generous grant from the Starbucks Foundation. The children that the program set out to feed were 500 learners from Grades 3 to 6—children identified as malnourished or undernourished. Many of them come from families relocated from the railroad tracks. They were coming to school on empty stomachs, and because they were hungry, it was very difficult for them to learn.

For 38 school days—from Jan. 26 to March 19, 2026—the Loaves and Fish kitchen cooked fresh, nutritious meals every single morning. Parent volunteers from a private school, PAREF Southridge, delivered the meals to the school. Teachers and the school nurse watched over every child every single school day. At the end of those 38 days, the children were subjected to health measurements: ninety-five percent (95 percent) of the 500 children gained weight. Furthermore, every subject—English, Filipino, Science, Mathematics, and Araling Panlipunan—showed higher test scores in the fourth quarter than in the quarter prior to when the feeding started.

Children who used to arrive tired and distracted became more alert. Children with frequent absences started showing up daily—because for some of them, the meal served in school was the only decent meal for the whole day. One child told a teacher, “I am excited to come to school now.” That child, fed, healthy, and learning today, is the nurse, the engineer, the teacher, or the entrepreneur of tomorrow. The Philippine Food Bank spent just 57 centavos per meal to invest in the human resources of tomorrow, thanks to the donation of surplus food, dedicated volunteers, and the quiet faith of sponsors who agreed to help even before they knew the outcome.

Fortunately, the Starbucks Foundation has generously invited the Philippine Food Bank to apply for a second grant. The officials, with the support of numerous donors—among them those who participated in the Golf Tournament at Tagaytay Midlands—have every intention of going beyond one grant and one school. The Balik Lusog program resumed at Poblacion Elementary School in Muntinlupa on July 27, 2026, the exact same day that President Marcos delivered his SONA. Close to 1,000 undernourished children in Grades two to six will once again be fed for as many days as possible during the school year.

From there, the Foundation plans to bring Balik Lusog to every public elementary school in Muntinlupa, hopefully in partnership with the School-Based Feeding Program of the Department of Education. The Foundation is now in conversations with officials from the Department of Education so that a formal Public-Private Partnership framework can be developed on the basis of our experience at the elementary school in Muntinlupa. Our next target is the City of Pasig, where two leading government officials, Mayor Vico Sotto and Congressman Roman Romulo, are among the most enlightened on this long-festering problem of child undernutrition and its very deleterious effect on the quality of our human resources.

After the Foundation perfects the Muntinlupa and Pasig models, there is no limit to what can be accomplished across the numerous Philippine municipalities. We hope the Balik Lusog experiment in Muntinlupa can inspire other private initiatives combating hunger in the Philippines to adopt the PPP model, ensuring government funds are best utilized with a minimum of inefficiency and poor governance.

I am especially referring to several notable private initiatives. Among corporate foundation feeding programs, many large Philippine enterprises operate long-term nutrition programs through their foundations, including the Jollibee Group Foundation (Busog, Lusog, Talino—BLT—feeding program and community kitchens), Pilipinas Shell Foundation (school-community nutrition projects), Ayala Foundation (nutrition and maternal-child health initiatives), Aboitiz Foundation (community feeding and nutrition education), Metrobank Foundation (support for nutrition and health programs), Manila Water Foundation (nutrition linked to clean water and sanitation), ABS-CBN Lingkod Kapamilya Foundation (feeding and nutrition assistance), and GMA Kapuso Foundation (nutrition and disaster feeding).

Faith-based organizations also play a vital role, including Caritas Philippines, Feed the Hungry Philippines, various Catholic diocesan feeding programs, and several Protestant and Evangelical feeding groups. Similarly, NGO-led nutrition programs contribute immensely to the cause, such as the Philippine Food Bank Foundation, Rise Against Hunger, Project PEARLS, Kabisig ng Kalahi, Gawad Kalinga, and the NVC Foundation, whose Mingo nutrition program provides fortified complementary food to undernourished children.

I have by no means prepared an exhaustive list of private initiatives that directly address the serious problem of undernourished children. In fact, it can be arguably stated that the Philippines has one of Southeast Asia’s broadest networks of private-sector nutrition initiatives. Corporate foundations, NGOs, churches, civic organizations, and international partners collectively invest hundreds of millions of pesos each year in feeding programs, nutrition, food fortification, community kitchens, breastfeeding promotion, and livelihood initiatives.

title: Promises, performance, and the 'mahiya naman kayo' moment
content_lead:
As we prepare to listen to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s State of the Nation Address this afternoon, it is only fitting to look back at what was promised -- and what has been delivered -- since the 2025 SONA. Last year's address was defined by bold commitments: ₱20 rice, zero-balance billing in hospitals, lifeline electricity rates, and expanded support for small businesses. Today, as we evaluate the administration's progress, the measure of this SONA will not be found in applause lines, but in whether performance has caught up with promise.

When President Marcos Jr. delivered his 2025 State of the Nation Address, he chose to speak less of promises and more of performance. It was a deliberate pivot: a leader entering the final stretch of his term, conscious that history will judge him not by rhetoric but by delivery.

However, the numbers in 2026 tell a more complex story than the optimism of a year ago. While the 2025 address offered hope, the current economic landscape faces significant headwinds. Inflation, which had tempered to 1.4 percent by June 2025, has proven stubborn, rising to 6.4 percent in June 2026. This remains consistently above the central bank's 2-4 percent target, keeping the cost of living high for ordinary families. Furthermore, core inflation -- which strips away volatile items -- reached 4.4 percent in June, the highest in 31 months, signaling that price pressures have become broad-based.

The findings come from surveys done 10 years earlier, however, and mounting pressures on the area's forests since then may have had an impact, the authors say.

As the last remaining natural lowland forest in Cavite province, on the southern shores of Manila Bay, Mounts Palay-palay-Mataas-na-Gulod Protected Landscape serves as a vital stronghold for Philippine biodiversity, researchers say.

In July 2016, they surveyed plants within the landscape, known as MPPMGPL. At the time, they documented 294 species of plants across the landscape's varied habitats, from grasslands and secondary forests to old-growth stands. They found that 42 species, or 16%, are found only in the Philippines, while 31 species are classified as threatened on national or international red lists.

"The most remarkable finding is that this landscape ... harbors an incredibly high concentration of biodiversity despite being so close to highly urbanized zones," study lead author Enrico Replan, an assistant professor at the Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology (IESM) at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told Mongabay by email.

The study also identified 43 species that likely represent new records for Cavite province, "filling major geographic knowledge gaps," Replan said. Among the most significant findings was the dominance of guijo (Shorea guiso), a critically endangered tree species, in the forest's interior core. This highlights the role of MPPMGPL as a key conservation refuge, the authors write.

title: Victory! Illegal Horse Race Cancelled In Laguna After PETA Push | Journal Online
content_lead:
Manila -- In a groundbreaking victory for horses, authorities in Liliw, Laguna, have cancelled an illegal horse race that was scheduled to take place on 25 July -- taking action within 24 hours after PETA alerted them that the event would expose horses to significant risks of injury, exhaustion, and stress. This marks the first time in the country that authorities have successfully stopped an illegal horse race before it could take place.

In its letter to Mayor Ildefonso Monleon, PETA noted that the event -- which was planned as part of fiesta celebration at a barangay in Liliw -- would likely violate the Animal Welfare Act and was being conducted outside the regulatory authority of the Philippine Racing Commission. PETA also contacted several government agencies -- including the Bureau of Animal Industry, the Municipal Agriculture, and the Philippine National Police local offices in Liliw -- and the authorities acted swiftly to cancel the race.

"This is a historic moment for horses in the Philippines and shows what can be achieved when authorities prioritize animal welfare," says PETA President Jason Baker. "PETA urges other local governments across the country to follow Liliw's compassionate example and prevent dangerous horse races from taking place in their jurisdictions."

Horses used for racing are forced to sprint at speeds so fast that they frequently sustain catastrophic and often fatal injuries. When they stop winning races, many horses are killed.

PETA -- whose motto reads, in part, that "animals are not ours to use for entertainment" -- points out that when it comes to the ability to feel pain, hunger, and fear, a horse is a dog is a boy. title: Searca highlights climate-resilient farming, promising ube varieties
content_lead:
LOS BAÑOS, Laguna -- Long prized as a staple in Filipino culinary tradition, purple yam -- locally known as ube -- is emerging as a key driver of agricultural growth and climate resilience for smallholder farmers.

Insights featured in the Agriculture and Development Seminar Series (ADSS) organized by the Southeast Asian Regional Center for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture (Searca) show that while global and domestic demand for ube continues to surge, local supply struggles to keep pace, creating a significant opportunity to transform traditional root-crop farming into a highly profitable enterprise.

Market demand remains strong, with ube exports generating $3.06 million in 2025 through sought-after processed products such as powders, purees, and traditional pastes (halaya).

However, domestic production reached only about 13,535 metric tons in 2022, compared with a national demand of 49,000 metric tons. Low baseline yields, seasonal crop behavior, tuber dormancy, and a shortage of quality planting materials continue to limit overall production.

To bridge this gap, agricultural frameworks under the High Value Crops Development Program (HVCDP) of the Department of Agriculture (DA) are prioritizing crop resilience and diversification.

title: Laguna de Bay agency seeks public's help to trace polluters

LUCENA CITY - The Laguna Lake Development Authority (LLDA) has appealed to the public to help identify the sources of pollution in Laguna de Bay, saying community reports are crucial in holding environmental violators accountable.

In a public advisory issued Sunday, July 19, the LLDA acknowledged the role of residents and local officials in reporting signs of possible water contamination, including heavy bubbling or foaming on river surfaces, unusual water discoloration, and foul odors.

"The LLDA acknowledges the quick response of communities in reporting the immediate impacts of water contamination," the agency said.

The advisory was issued days after the LLDA permanently sealed the discharge outlet used by Manila Water Company Inc. (MWCI) in Binangonan, Rizal, following a controversial pipeline flushing operation.

The agency said the measure was intended to prevent similar discharges while its investigation continues.

The LLDA has yet to determine whether the flushing operation was linked to the reported fish kill on the Rizal side of Laguna de Bay. Investigators are still assessing the volume and quality of the discharged water through sampling and field inspections.

title: Laguna Bluebelt's photo contest displays local ocean beauty
content_lead:
Stunning images that celebrate the diversity of wildlife and ocean habitat found along Laguna Beach's protected shoreline are on display for a limited time.

The Laguna Bluebelt Coalition recently recognized amateur and professional photographers in its 15th annual Bluebelt Photo Contest. The event held at the LCAD Gallery along Ocean Avenue awarded prizes to photographers in several categories. Their photos are on display through Aug. 16.

The purpose of the contest is to recognize and celebrate the natural wonders off the Laguna Beach coastline, with a special emphasis on the Marine Protected Areas, which are designated beaches, coves and rock outcroppings along five miles of the town where no wildlife, rock, shell, crustacean, or fish can be touched or removed.

"The photo contest documents the animals and the habitat that's in the Marine Protected Areas," said Anne Girtz, a civil engineer and member of the Bluebelt Coalition. "It's this citizen scientist and documentation of the value and the diversity of critters that are in (the MPA) areas."

This year's winning photographers include Jordan Manning, of Dana Point, who received first place in the professional category with a photo capturing a moment beneath the kelp where he encountered a curious harbor seal.

title: Marcos distributes cash aid to Lucena scholars
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY -- President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. handed out cash assistance to 165 presidential scholars currently enrolled in private colleges in this city on Tuesday here at the Lucena Convention Center.

Each student received a one-time P20,000 educational assistance under the Bagong Pilipinas Barangay Presidential Scholars Program.

Marcos said this grassroot project is aimed at strengthening the education capability of students and to curb the increasing number of learners who are forced to stop schooling due to lack of financial support.

"This privilege is funded by the Local Government Support Fund, enabling all local government units to provide adequate education opportunities to our young residents," Marcos said.

The program is a national government initiative where each barangay may have five scholars.

Marcos also led the distribution of a 10-kilo sack of rice for each of the 52,400 indigent households in Lucena under the "Bigay Bigas sa Masa" initiative.

The rice distribution is part of the Sagip Saka Act with the government directly buying harvested rice from local farmers and distributing it to vulnerable sectors.

Also present during the distribution were Lucena Mayor Mark Alcala, Quezon Gov. Helen Tan and Vice Gov. Anacleto Alcala III.

Marcos also led the distribution of the Certificate of Entitlement under Presidential Proclamation 436, Series of 2003, that provides urban poor families and city government employees their own parcel of land in Barangay Ibabang Iyam, a 17.6-hectare property previously owned by the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines.

title: DAR distributes P5.49M in farm machinery to Calabarzon beneficiaries
content_lead:
THE Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) on Sunday said it distributed P5.49 million worth of farm machinery and equipment to beneficiaries and farmer organizations in the provinces of Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, and Quezon (Calabarzon).

DAR Undersecretary for Field Operations Kazel Celeste led the turnover on July 21 in Lucena. The distribution was part of DAR's agrarian reform program, which also included the awarding of certificates of land ownership, certificates of condonation and release of mortgage, and electronic titles under the Support to Parcelization of Lands for Individual Titling project.

Batangas received P1.98 million worth of equipment, including a 40-horsepower, four-wheel-drive tractor with rotary tiller and disc plow, three motorcycles with carriers, weighing scales and powered pressure washers.

Cavite got a 50-horsepower, four-wheel tractor worth P1.47 million.

Quezon I was given a motorcycle with sidecar and a hand tractor worth P300,000, while Quezon II received a multi-tiller, ride-on mini combine harvester, mechanical rice transplanter, grass cutters and knapsack sprayers worth P1.75 million.

title: 'Habagat' rains affect 3,640 families in Rizal, Cavite, Batangas
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY, Philippines - Heavy rains brought by Tropical Depression Maymay and the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat, have affected 3,640 families in the provinces of Rizal, Cavite, and Batangas, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said Sunday, Aug.9.

"Based on the reports received by the field office from affected local government units, there are already 3,640 affected families in 50 barangays in the provinces of Rizal, Cavite and Batangas," the DSWD Calabarzon Field Office said in a report Sunday noon.

More than 400 of the affected families were staying in 27 evacuation centers opened and managed by their respective local government units (LGUs), the agency added.

READ: Habagat brings heavy rains, flooding in parts of PH

The DSWD field office continued to monitor the effects of the southwest monsoon and Maymay across the Calabarzon Region.

Maymay had dissipated into a low-pressure area and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility on Friday, along with Typhoon Dolphin. However, the southwest monsoon continued to bring rains over parts of Luzon.

The DSWD said its field offices throughout the region were ready to provide disaster-response augmentation to affected LGUs, while provincial, city, and municipal quick response teams had remained on standby since Aug. 5.

As of August 6, DSWD Calabarzon had strategically prepositioned 227,216 family food packs worth P148.27 million, 11,630 ready-to-eat food packs worth P8.88 million, and 11,119 non-food items worth P21.57 million in 78 warehouses across the region.

The field office also had P3 million in standby funds to facilitate the immediate procurement of additional relief goods and other essential resources should the need arise.

The DSWD urged affected LGUs and communities to remain vigilant and continue coordinating with disaster response authorities as weather conditions develop. /atm

A total of 22 teams participated this year, competing for permit, bonefish, and tarpon on the island's pristine fly-fishing flats. At the end of the three-day competition, Team Robb's Red Rumm emerged as the champions. The team also claimed the grand prize last year, when competing under the name One Shot Willy's.

The tournament is more than a competition; it provides an opportunity to raise much-needed funds for educational and environmental programs. A 50/50 raffle raised more than $1,600 for the Belize Flats Fisher Association, along with an additional $800 donated by the tournament. Dr. Addiel Perez of the Bonefish & Tarpon Trust thanked everyone who supported the event and presented a $6,080 donation to his organization. Meanwhile, Omar Arceo's Youth Fly Fishing Program also received a $6,080 donation. Tournament President Tina Winkler and fellow Master of Ceremonies Marisela Marin said these contributions support conservation efforts and youth development in San Pedro.

Throughout the tournament, while anglers were busy fishing the flats, pop-up markets at Central Park offered food, drinks, and music. Evening activities were also held for children interested in learning about fly-fishing. Arceo, affectionately known as the "Dr. of the Flats," taught participants about this form of sport fishing and its significant contribution to the tourism industry. With support from sponsors such as Blue Bonefish Lodge, several young anglers were introduced to the sport while learning about the importance of conservation. Participants also took home prizes.

title: UPLIFT beneficiaries allocate cash aid for food, medicine, home repairs
content_lead:
Beneficiaries of the UPLIFT cash aid program said the money would go to food, medicine, and home repairs.

Beneficiaries of the government's expanded Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) program began claiming their cash aid on Monday, saying they will spend it on daily necessities and house repairs in preparation for the rainy season.

In Oscar Oida's "24 Oras" report, the cash aid distribution, spearheaded by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), was simultaneously held across the country.

In Muntinlupa City, Luzviminda Gemina, 68, said that qualifying as a UPLIFT beneficiary was an "answered prayer," because she can finally fix their house, especially their roof that is full of holes.

"Nagulat na nga lang ako eh sa tagal ng panahon, ngayon lang ako nakatanggap. Nakatanggap man ako, sir, e bigas sa senior. Sakto po na makabili akong yero, kahit tatlo lang muna kasi ang kailangan na yero sa bahay ko, anim," Gemina said.

(I was surprised because this is the first time I've received something like this. Before, I only received the rice allowance for seniors. This is just in time for me to buy roofing sheets -- even just three for now, because my house actually needs six.)

Around 43 beneficiaries from Muntinlupa City received their P2,000 cash assistance on Monday. They were the only ones who showed up out of the 124 individuals who qualified in the program based on the Philippine Statistics Authority's 2024 community-based monitoring system.

According to local authorities, some of the qualified individuals can no longer be located.

"'Yung iba naman po nakakulong, 'yung iba nasa probinsya na po. Talagang mostly wala na po sila dito sa Muntinlupa," said Maritess Dumasena of the Social Service Department of Muntinlupa City.

title: Siblings cooking lunch killed in Rizal rockslide
content_lead:
Two siblings, aged 22 and 20, were killed after a boulder struck them while they were cooking lunch at the store where they worked during a rockslide in Sitio Wawa, Barangay San Rafael, Rodriguez, Rizal, on Wednesday, Aug. 5.

On Thursday, Aug. 6, Barangay Captain Judith Cruz told the Manila Bulletin that the siblings were with the 22-year-old female victim's husband before the incident. He had briefly left to fish near the store when the rockslide occurred around 12 p.m.

"Nangyari po yung incident doon sa tindahan po yun na kanilang pinag t-trabahuan. Nung 12, nagluluto yung magkapatid para sa tanghalian nila (The incident happened at the store where they worked. At around noon, the siblings were cooking their lunch when the incident occurred)," she said.

Cruz said the impact of the falling boulder was so strong that it hurled the female victim's body into the river, while her brother allegedly sustained fatal injuries.

She added that the boulder may have fallen from higher up, as there were reportedly no sounds of falling rocks before the incident. Only a single boulder was reported to have fallen.

"Walang narinig na parang nag-slide na bato, parang biglang deretso bagsak. So big sabihin (baka) ang taas ng pinanggalingan (There were no sounds of rocks sliding. It was as if the boulder suddenly fell straight down, so it may have come from much higher up)," she said.

Only the store where the victims were working at the time of the incident was affected by the falling boulder.

Cruz said the victims had also survived a rockslide last year, during which a boulder struck their home, although all members of the family escaped unharmed. She added that they had been advised to relocate from the area, but still went to Sitio Wawa for work.

She said she was saddened by the incident, noting that she had personally met and spoken with the female victim only recently, who was among those who received school supplies and rice from the barangay.

title: Budget release rate hits 88% at end-June
content_lead:
THE Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said it released 87.9% of the budget for 2026 as of the end of June.

According to the DBM Status of Allotment Release report, the releases amounted to P5.97 trillion out of the original budget total of P6.79 trillion, leaving P819.49 billion undistributed.

The release rate at the end of last month was running behind the year-earlier pace of 90%.

Releases to government agencies and departments amounted to P3.34 trillion by the end of June, equivalent to 90.9% of their allocations, compared to 94% in the same period last year.

Special-purpose funds released by the end of the month stood at P477 billion, representing 66.3% of the total allotment.

Meanwhile, automatic appropriation releases were at 89.8%, or P2.15 trillion.

These include the National Tax Allotment of P1.19 trillion, the P712.5 billion in interest payments, the P93.98 billion for the Block Grant, the P82.92 billion for retirement and life insurance premiums, and the P36.47 billion for a special account in the general fund, which includes the P6 billion allotment for the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement program.

"Other" releases amounted to P134.84 billion, which include continuing appropriations from last year worth P22.76 billion, P85.65 billion in unprogrammed appropriations, and other automatic appropriations worth P26.43 billion.

title: First 2,000 days seen as key to healthier childhood | Rizal Raoul Reyes
content_lead:
Providing children with balanced nutrition during their first 2,000 days, from pregnancy through early childhood, can help lay the foundation for better health and development, according to Nestlé Philippines.

The first 1,000 days, covering pregnancy through a child's second birthday, has long been recognized as a critical period for establishing lifelong health. But Nestlé Philippines is also looking at the succeeding years, arguing that opportunities to improve children's nutritional status extend beyond age two.

"The first 1,000 days is indeed very important," said Edelweiss Sicat, nutrition advocacy lead of Nestlé Philippines, during a recent media roundtable in Makati City. She noted, however, that appropriate nutrition, fortification and healthier food choices can continue to support children's development in the years that follow.

Jose Uy III, senior vice president and head of corporate affairs at Nestlé Philippines, emphasized that the broader focus does not diminish the importance of the first 1,000 days.

Cha Sy, corporate nutritionist at Nestlé Wellness Campus and project lead, said efforts could include food fortification and expanding access to products that contribute to children's nutritional needs.

The company also reiterated that breastfeeding remains the best option for infants. Uy said breast-milk substitutes are intended for situations in which mothers are medically unable to provide sufficient breast milk.

Beyond nutrition

The discussion also highlighted the role of added sugar and overall lifestyle in children's health.

Sy stressed the importance of limiting added sugars as part of a healthier diet. For a 2,000-calorie daily diet, Sicat said the commonly cited limit for added sugars is about 50 grams, or roughly 10 teaspoons. This refers to sugars added to foods, such as table sugar and honey, rather than naturally occurring sugars in whole foods.
